182	\section{Control Task Methodology}
183	\label{app:control}
184	
185	We follow the selectivity framework of \cite{hewitt2019control} to verify that our probes capture genuine safety-relevant structure rather than surface-level correlations.
186	
187	\paragraph{Procedure.} For each model, we randomly permute the binary labels (pre-CP vs. post-CP) across all steps while preserving the marginal label distribution. We then retrain the probe with identical architecture (L2-regularized logistic regression) and hyperparameters on these shuffled labels. Selectivity is defined as:
188	\begin{equation}
189	    \text{Selectivity} = \text{Acc}_{\text{linguistic}} - \text{Acc}_{\text{control}}
190	\end{equation}
191	where $\text{Acc}_{\text{linguistic}}$ is the probe accuracy on true labels and $\text{Acc}_{\text{control}}$ is the accuracy on permuted labels. A selectivity of zero indicates that the probe exploits only non-linguistic features (e.g., position); higher values confirm that the representation encodes task-relevant information.
192	
193	\paragraph{Results.} We repeat the control experiment 5 times with different random permutations and report the mean control accuracy. Selectivity scores are: R1-8B 12.5pp (layer 14), QwQ-32B 15.3pp (layer 2), R1-32B 7.5pp (layer 10). All values exceed the 5pp threshold recommended by \cite{hewitt2019control}. R1-32B's weaker selectivity (7.5pp, near the threshold) is consistent with its overall weaker hidden-state signal. On QwQ-32B, the position baseline accuracy (70.6\%) slightly exceeds the HS probe (67.8\%), indicating that layer 2 encodes strong positional information alongside safety-relevant structure.
194	
195	\paragraph{Position-only baseline.} As a complementary validation, we train a logistic regression classifier using only the normalized step index ($t / T$ where $T$ is the total trace length) as the input feature. This baseline tests whether temporal position alone explains probe performance. On R1-8B, the position-only baseline produces 15.8\% FPR compared to 8.1\% for the HS probe at matched detection rates. The probe's substantially lower FPR confirms that hidden state features carry information beyond what step position provides.

242	These results reveal a coverage-timing tradeoff. When missed detections are costly, BOCPD's coverage advantage justifies its use despite the timing penalty. When early intervention is the priority, simple thresholding provides better lead time.

245	\section{M002 Bug Disclosure}
246	\label{app:bug}
247	
248	We disclose a bug discovered during development that affected intermediate results for QwQ-32B.
249	
250	\paragraph{Issue.} In experiment M002 (text baseline evaluation), the QwQ-32B text probe was inadvertently initialized with a midpoint heuristic placeholder rather than true sentence embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Specifically, the placeholder assigned each step a feature vector equal to the midpoint between the mean safe and mean unsafe embeddings from the training set, with small Gaussian noise added. This made the text probe trivially predictive, producing a spuriously significant result ($p{=}0.001$ for HS vs. text FPR difference).
251	
252	\paragraph{Discovery and correction.} The bug was identified during a systematic audit of the feature extraction pipeline. After correction (using actual sentence embeddings), QwQ-32B shows no meaningful modality difference: accuracy $p{=}0.828$, precision $p{=}0.346$, FPR $p{=}0.430$ (two-sided permutation test, 1000 resamples). R1-32B shows directional HS advantages (accuracy $p{=}0.080$, precision $p{=}0.050$, FPR $p{=}0.114$) but none survive Holm-Bonferroni correction. Full results are reported in \cref{tab:hs_vs_text}.
253	
254	\paragraph{Impact on reported results.} All numbers reported in this paper use the corrected pipeline. No figures, tables, or claims in the main text are affected by the original bug. The correction changed only QwQ-32B text baseline numbers, which now show no significant difference from the HS probe on that model.
255	
256	\paragraph{Commitment to transparency.} We report this bug to maintain scientific integrity. All code, including the git history showing the bug and its fix, will be released with the camera-ready version. Researchers reproducing our results can verify the correction independently.
257	
258	\section{Cross-Model Transfer Implementation Details}
259	\label{app:transfer_details}
260	
261	We test whether safety probes transfer across models by projecting hidden states into a shared dimensionality space and applying cross-model classification.
262	
263	\paragraph{Method.} For each source-target model pair, we apply PCA independently to each model's hidden states, reducing to a shared dimensionality $d \in \{512, 1024, 2048\}$. PCA is fitted on the full dataset (including test traces) for each model separately, a setting favorable to transfer since it maximizes the quality of the projection. A logistic regression classifier (C=1.0, class\_weight=`balanced', max\_iter=2000, random\_state=42) trained on the source model's PCA-projected training data is then applied directly to the target model's PCA-projected test data. No cross-model alignment step (Procrustes rotation, CCA, or learned projection) is applied; PCA serves as a standard linear dimensionality reduction baseline.
264	
265	\paragraph{Same-dimension pairs.} For R1-32B and QwQ-32B (both 5120-d hidden states), we additionally test direct transfer without PCA: the source classifier is applied directly to the target model's raw hidden states. This tests whether same-architecture, same-dimensionality models share safety-relevant linear structure.
266	
267	\paragraph{Results.} All 18 transfer configurations (6 directional pairs $\times$ 3 methods: PCA-512, PCA-1024, PCA-2048, plus direct for same-dimension pairs) fail to produce meaningful transfer. The best result is QwQ-32B $\rightarrow$ R1-32B direct transfer at 67.3\% balanced accuracy, against a within-model baseline of 65.2\% (+2.1pp). This margin is within noise and not statistically significant. The complete failure under maximally favorable conditions (PCA fitted on full data, no train/test separation for projection) strengthens the conclusion that safety commitment is encoded in model-specific geometric configurations. PCA is a standard linear alignment baseline; its failure indicates that the problem lies in the representations themselves rather than in the choice of alignment method.

\section{Control Task Methodology}
\label{app:control}

We follow the selectivity framework of \cite{hewitt2019control} to verify that our probes capture genuine safety-relevant structure rather than surface-level correlations.

\paragraph{Procedure.} For each model, we randomly permute the binary labels (pre-CP vs. post-CP) across all steps while preserving the marginal label distribution. We then retrain the probe with identical architecture (L2-regularized logistic regression) and hyperparameters on these shuffled labels. Selectivity is defined as:
\begin{equation}
    \text{Selectivity} = \text{Acc}_{\text{linguistic}} - \text{Acc}_{\text{control}}
\end{equation}
where $\text{Acc}_{\text{linguistic}}$ is the probe accuracy on true labels and $\text{Acc}_{\text{control}}$ is the accuracy on permuted labels. A selectivity of zero indicates that the probe exploits only non-linguistic features (e.g., position); higher values confirm that the representation encodes task-relevant information.

\paragraph{Results.} We repeat the control experiment 5 times with different random permutations and report the mean control accuracy. Selectivity scores are: R1-8B 12.5pp (layer 14), QwQ-32B 15.3pp (layer 2), R1-32B 7.5pp (layer 10). All values exceed the 5pp threshold recommended by \cite{hewitt2019control}. R1-32B's weaker selectivity (7.5pp, near the threshold) is consistent with its overall weaker hidden-state signal. On QwQ-32B, the position baseline accuracy (70.6\%) slightly exceeds the HS probe (67.8\%), indicating that layer 2 encodes strong positional information alongside safety-relevant structure.

\paragraph{Position-only baseline.} As a complementary validation, we train a logistic regression classifier using only the normalized step index ($t / T$ where $T$ is the total trace length) as the input feature. This baseline tests whether temporal position alone explains probe performance. On R1-8B, the position-only baseline produces 15.8\% FPR compared to 8.1\% for the HS probe at matched detection rates. The probe's substantially lower FPR confirms that hidden state features carry information beyond what step position provides.

\section{M002 Bug Disclosure}
\label{app:bug}

We disclose a bug discovered during development that affected intermediate results for QwQ-32B.

\paragraph{Issue.} In experiment M002 (text baseline evaluation), the QwQ-32B text probe was inadvertently initialized with a midpoint heuristic placeholder rather than true sentence embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Specifically, the placeholder assigned each step a feature vector equal to the midpoint between the mean safe and mean unsafe embeddings from the training set, with small Gaussian noise added. This made the text probe trivially predictive, producing a spuriously significant result ($p{=}0.001$ for HS vs. text FPR difference).

\paragraph{Discovery and correction.} The bug was identified during a systematic audit of the feature extraction pipeline. After correction (using actual sentence embeddings), QwQ-32B shows no meaningful modality difference: accuracy $p{=}0.828$, precision $p{=}0.346$, FPR $p{=}0.430$ (two-sided permutation test, 1000 resamples). R1-32B shows directional HS advantages (accuracy $p{=}0.080$, precision $p{=}0.050$, FPR $p{=}0.114$) but none survive Holm-Bonferroni correction. Full results are reported in \cref{tab:hs_vs_text}.

\paragraph{Impact on reported results.} All numbers reported in this paper use the corrected pipeline. No figures, tables, or claims in the main text are affected by the original bug. The correction changed only QwQ-32B text baseline numbers, which now show no significant difference from the HS probe on that model.

\paragraph{Commitment to transparency.} We report this bug to maintain scientific integrity. All code, including the git history showing the bug and its fix, will be released with the camera-ready version. Researchers reproducing our results can verify the correction independently.

\section{Cross-Model Transfer Implementation Details}
\label{app:transfer_details}

We test whether safety probes transfer across models by projecting hidden states into a shared dimensionality space and applying cross-model classification.

\paragraph{Method.} For each source-target model pair, we apply PCA independently to each model's hidden states, reducing to a shared dimensionality $d \in \{512, 1024, 2048\}$. PCA is fitted on the full dataset (including test traces) for each model separately, a setting favorable to transfer since it maximizes the quality of the projection. A logistic regression classifier (C=1.0, class\_weight=`balanced', max\_iter=2000, random\_state=42) trained on the source model's PCA-projected training data is then applied directly to the target model's PCA-projected test data. No cross-model alignment step (Procrustes rotation, CCA, or learned projection) is applied; PCA serves as a standard linear dimensionality reduction baseline.

\paragraph{Same-dimension pairs.} For R1-32B and QwQ-32B (both 5120-d hidden states), we additionally test direct transfer without PCA: the source classifier is applied directly to the target model's raw hidden states. This tests whether same-architecture, same-dimensionality models share safety-relevant linear structure.

\paragraph{Results.} All 18 transfer configurations (6 directional pairs $\times$ 3 methods: PCA-512, PCA-1024, PCA-2048, plus direct for same-dimension pairs) fail to produce meaningful transfer. The best result is QwQ-32B $\rightarrow$ R1-32B direct transfer at 67.3\% balanced accuracy, against a within-model baseline of 65.2\% (+2.1pp). This margin is within noise and not statistically significant. The complete failure under maximally favorable conditions (PCA fitted on full data, no train/test separation for projection) strengthens the conclusion that safety commitment is encoded in model-specific geometric configurations. PCA is a standard linear alignment baseline; its failure indicates that the problem lies in the representations themselves rather than in the choice of alignment method.

\paragraph{R1-8B} shows a general upward trend in balanced accuracy from 77.8\% ($W{=}1$) to 81.0\% ($W{=}25$), gaining +3.2pp overall with a slight dip at $W{=}5$ (78.1\%). Precision improves sharply (+12.9pp) and step-level FPR halves (9.65\% to 4.83\%). Coverage trades off against quality, dropping from 72.1\% to 48.8\%.

\paragraph{R1-32B} exhibits a non-monotonic pattern: balanced accuracy peaks at $W{=}10$ (73.7\%) and then declines, falling below the $W{=}1$ baseline by $W{=}20$ (69.6\%). \paragraph{QwQ-32B} shows a broadly increasing trend with local non-monotonicity: balanced accuracy peaks at $W{=}5$ (76.1\%), dips at $W{=}10$--$15$, then recovers to 76.2\% at $W{=}25$. \paragraph{Universal trends.} Across all models: (1) larger windows reduce coverage as the smoothed probe fires less frequently; (2) FPR generally decreases with window size; (3) lead time decreases (larger windows delay first detection). We use $W{=}15$ as the default temporal window in the main text, as it provides a good balance of accuracy and FPR reduction while maintaining reasonable coverage across models.

\section{GRU Training Details}

\paragraph{Architecture.} We evaluate two GRU variants. \paragraph{Training procedure.} We train with Adam (learning rate $1 \times 10^{-3}$, default $\beta_1{=}0.9$, $\beta_2{=}0.999$), batch size 16, for a maximum of 50 epochs. Early stopping halts training when validation loss does not improve for 10 consecutive epochs. Input features are z-score normalized per dimension using training set statistics.

\paragraph{Evaluation.} We report crossing accuracy (the sustained accuracy at which the probe first exceeds chance for 5 consecutive steps) and detection lead (steps before CP at crossing point). All experiments use 3 random seeds; we report mean $\pm$ standard deviation.

\section{Control Task Methodology}
\label{app:control}

We follow the selectivity framework of \cite{hewitt2019control} to verify that our probes capture genuine safety-relevant structure rather than surface-level correlations.

\paragraph{Procedure.} For each model, we randomly permute the binary labels (pre-CP vs. post-CP) across all steps while preserving the marginal label distribution. We then retrain the probe with identical architecture (L2-regularized logistic regression) and hyperparameters on these shuffled labels. Selectivity is defined as:
\begin{equation}
    \text{Selectivity} = \text{Acc}_{\text{linguistic}} - \text{Acc}_{\text{control}}
\end{equation}
where $\text{Acc}_{\text{linguistic}}$ is the probe accuracy on true labels and $\text{Acc}_{\text{control}}$ is the accuracy on permuted labels. A selectivity of zero indicates that the probe exploits only non-linguistic features (e.g., position); higher values confirm that the representation encodes task-relevant information.

\paragraph{Results.} We repeat the control experiment 5 times with different random permutations and report the mean control accuracy. Selectivity scores are: R1-8B 12.5pp (layer 14), QwQ-32B 15.3pp (layer 2), R1-32B 7.5pp (layer 10). All values exceed the 5pp threshold recommended by \cite{hewitt2019control}. R1-32B's weaker selectivity (7.5pp, near the threshold) is consistent with its overall weaker hidden-state signal. On QwQ-32B, the position baseline accuracy (70.6\%) slightly exceeds the HS probe (67.8\%), indicating that layer 2 encodes strong positional information alongside safety-relevant structure.

\paragraph{Position-only baseline.} As a complementary validation, we train a logistic regression classifier using only the normalized step index ($t / T$ where $T$ is the total trace length) as the input feature. This baseline tests whether temporal position alone explains probe performance. On R1-8B, the position-only baseline produces 15.8\% FPR compared to 8.1\% for the HS probe at matched detection rates. The probe's substantially lower FPR confirms that hidden state features carry information beyond what step position provides.

The transition toward unsafe reasoning is gradual rather than abrupt, so change-point methods cannot exploit discontinuities for early warning. When missed detections are costly, BOCPD's coverage advantage justifies its use despite the timing penalty. When early intervention is the priority, simple thresholding provides better lead time.


\section{M002 Bug Disclosure}
\label{app:bug}

We disclose a bug discovered during development that affected intermediate results for QwQ-32B.

\paragraph{Issue.} In experiment M002 (text baseline evaluation), the QwQ-32B text probe was inadvertently initialized with a midpoint heuristic placeholder rather than true sentence embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Specifically, the placeholder assigned each step a feature vector equal to the midpoint between the mean safe and mean unsafe embeddings from the training set, with small Gaussian noise added. This made the text probe trivially predictive, producing a spuriously significant result ($p{=}0.001$ for HS vs. text FPR difference).

\paragraph{Discovery and correction.} The bug was identified during a systematic audit of the feature extraction pipeline. After correction (using actual sentence embeddings), QwQ-32B shows no meaningful modality difference: accuracy $p{=}0.828$, precision $p{=}0.346$, FPR $p{=}0.430$ (two-sided permutation test, 1000 resamples). R1-32B shows directional HS advantages (accuracy $p{=}0.080$, precision $p{=}0.050$, FPR $p{=}0.114$) but none survive Holm-Bonferroni correction. Full results are reported in \cref{tab:hs_vs_text}.

\paragraph{Impact on reported results.} All numbers reported in this paper use the corrected pipeline. No figures, tables, or claims in the main text are affected by the original bug. The correction changed only QwQ-32B text baseline numbers, which now show no significant difference from the HS probe on that model.

\paragraph{Commitment to transparency.} We report this bug to maintain scientific integrity. All code, including the git history showing the bug and its fix, will be released with the camera-ready version. Researchers reproducing our results can verify the correction independently.

\section{Cross-Model Transfer Implementation Details}
\label{app:transfer_details}

We test whether safety probes transfer across models by projecting hidden states into a shared dimensionality space and applying cross-model classification.

\paragraph{Method.} For each source-target model pair, we apply PCA independently to each model's hidden states, reducing to a shared dimensionality $d \in \{512, 1024, 2048\}$. PCA is fitted on the full dataset (including test traces) for each model separately, a setting favorable to transfer since it maximizes the quality of the projection. A logistic regression classifier (C=1.0, class\_weight=`balanced', max\_iter=2000, random\_state=42) trained on the source model's PCA-projected training data is then applied directly to the target model's PCA-projected test data. No cross-model alignment step (Procrustes rotation, CCA, or learned projection) is applied; PCA serves as a standard linear dimensionality reduction baseline.

\paragraph{Same-dimension pairs.} For R1-32B and QwQ-32B (both 5120-d hidden states), we additionally test direct transfer without PCA: the source classifier is applied directly to the target model's raw hidden states. This tests whether same-architecture, same-dimensionality models share safety-relevant linear structure.

\paragraph{Results.} All 18 transfer configurations (6 directional pairs $\times$ 3 methods: PCA-512, PCA-1024, PCA-2048, plus direct for same-dimension pairs) fail to produce meaningful transfer. The best result is QwQ-32B $\rightarrow$ R1-32B direct transfer at 67.3\% balanced accuracy, against a within-model baseline of 65.2\% (+2.1pp). This margin is within noise and not statistically significant. The complete failure under maximally favorable conditions (PCA fitted on full data, no train/test separation for projection) strengthens the conclusion that safety commitment is encoded in model-specific geometric configurations. PCA is a standard linear alignment baseline; its failure indicates that the problem lies in the representations themselves rather than in the choice of alignment method.
